protocol.name: wc_icon_v1

description.summary: icon pixels for an application id, from a resolver that is not the toplevel's client

protocol.description:
Wayland has no way for a *third party* to say what an application's icon is. xdg-toplevel-icon-v1 is the right protocol and the wrong shape for this project: it attaches an icon to an xdg_toplevel object, and a Wayland object belongs to exactly one client, so only the toplevel's own client can use it.
In the topology waycompose is built for (docs/goal-firefox.md) the client is on Linux, the compositor is on Windows, and the thing that knows what "firefox" looks like is neither of them: it is the XDG icon theme on the Linux side, which only wc-proxy can read. wc-proxy is a different client of this compositor from the application, and it cannot touch the application's objects.
So this interface is keyed by application id rather than by object. The resolver publishes pixels for an app id; the compositor applies them to every toplevel that has set that app id, now or later. Nothing here refers to a surface, and a publisher does not have to be running when the window it decorates appears.
Three things are deliberate:
- **Pixels, never a path or a name.** The whole point is that the filesystem holding the icon is on the other side of a hypervisor (docs/design.md §2.1). A request carrying a file name would work on one machine and be unimplementable on the one that matters. - **No wl_buffer, so no file descriptor.** An icon is a few kilobytes sent once per application. Routing it through a wl_shm pool would put an fd-shaped argument on a wire that must never carry one, to save a copy nobody can measure. - **Chunked, because a Wayland message is bounded.** wayland-backend's receive buffer is 4096 bytes (rs/mod.rs, DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE) and a 48x48 BGRA image is 9216, so the array has to arrive in pieces. That is a measured limit rather than a defensive one.

interface.name: wc_icon_manager_v1

description.summary: publishes icon pixels for application ids

interface.description:
An icon is built up out of band and then named: chunk* image, repeated once per size, and finally publish, which installs the whole set against an app id and empties the staging area.
A publish replaces whatever was there before. There is no way to ask what is installed: this is a one-directional feed from something that knows to something that draws.

entry.name: too_big
entry.summary: more staged bytes than the compositor will hold

entry.name: short_image
entry.summary: image named a size larger than the bytes that were staged

entry.name: bad_size
entry.summary: a non-positive or implausible width or height

request.name: destroy
request.description: Icons already published stay published. Destroying the manager does not take back what it said, because a window that has an icon should not lose it when the resolver exits.

request.name: chunk

description.summary: append bytes to the staging area

request.description:
Bytes are BGRA with **premultiplied** alpha, tightly packed, top row first — the layout the compositor's own shadow buffers use and the one wl_shm's ARGB8888 already specifies, so nothing has to be swizzled or multiplied between here and CreateIconIndirect. Windows agrees: a 32-bit icon bitmap is composited with AlphaBlend, which is defined on premultiplied colour.
A resolver decoding a PNG has to do the multiply itself, because PNG's alpha is straight. Getting that wrong shows up as a light halo around the icon rather than as an error.
Send as many chunks as the image needs. The split points carry no meaning; a row may span two chunks.

arg.name: data
arg.summary: a piece of the next image's pixels

request.name: image

description.summary: close off one image at this size

request.description: Consumes exactly width * height * 4 bytes from the front of the staging area and adds them to the set being built. Any remaining bytes stay staged for the next image, so a caller may send every size in one run of chunks if it likes.

request.name: publish

description.summary: install the staged set for an application id

request.description:
The app id is the string an xdg_toplevel gives to set_app_id, matched exactly. Publishing an empty set removes the entry, which is the difference between "this application has no icon" and "nobody has looked yet" — see forget.
Windows that already carry this app id are updated at once; windows that appear later pick it up when they are mapped.

request.name: forget

description.summary: drop what was published for an application id

request.description: Existing windows keep the icon they were given. This only stops the entry being applied to windows that have not appeared yet.
